newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CVRD sale awaits judge's ruling.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CVRD sale awaits judge's ruling.

text.p: Latin America's largest privatisation, the sale of Brazilian mining colossus Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, remained on hold Monday pending a key ruling from a high court judge.

A court spokeswoman said government lawyers had submitted documentation requested by Justice Democrito Reinaldo of the Superior Court of Justice in Brasilia, Brazil's highest tribunal for non-constitutional matters.
"The judge said he would judge in 24 hours," she said, adding it was possible Reinaldo could rule Monday.

Forty-five percent of CVRD's voting shares were due to have gone on the auction block at the Rio de Janeiro stock market on April 29 with a minimum price of $2.8 billion. But a flurry of court injunctions have repeatedly delayed the sale.
Reinaldo was due to rule on a government petition that all the lawsuits should be judged by a single tribunal because of a "conflict of interpretation" in lower courts.
Though a friend of Vice President Marco Maciel, Reinaldo has stressed he would not be swayed by political pressures.
He has also given the government no leeway at all. For example, he refused Friday night to accept the CVRD documents because they arrived 20 minutes after the court officially closed.
"In a way, it's turned out for the best because our lawyers could continue working on the documents all weekend and prepare the case," a spokeswoman for the government's Federal Advocacy said.
In Rio de Janeiro, officials were awaiting the green light from the judge, said a spokeswoman for the National Development Bank, which runs Brazil's privatisation programme.
Monday's O Globo newspaper said the delay was beginning to irritate the leader of one of the two consortiums bidding for control of the world's largest iron ore exporter.

"It's a very unpleasant situation," Globo quoted Antonio Ermirio de Moraes, chief executive of Brazilian conglomerate Votorantim, as saying. Votorantim heads the Valecom consortium, together with South Africa's Anglo American Corp.
Moraes said Brazil was putting on a "Third World show" and complained the delay was costing his partners money.
According to Globo, the government was also losing having had to spend $280,000 on the documents for its high court case alone.

An official at the court said Justice Democrito Reinaldo had agreed with the government's view, quashing all the injunctions included in the government's petition and naming a federal court in Rio de Janeiro as the tribunal responsible for all new cases.
Borges, however, said two or three injunctions remained.

"Tomorrow we will examine how best to overturn these injunctions," Borges told reporters, adding the government could either appeal to a federal court in Rio de Janeiro or ask the Superior Court of Justice to extend its ruling to the new cases.
Brazil hopes to raise at least $5.0 billion from the sale of the world's largest iron ore exporter, making it the biggest Latin American privatization to date.
But the sell-off of the jewel in the Brazilian public sector's crown has been controversial.
Demonstrators clashed with police in Rio last week and a chorus of criticism has risen from past presidents, Catholic bishops and the judiciary.
Monday's O Globo newspaper said the delay was beginning to irritate the leader of one of the two consortia bidding.
